stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
battery = 35
if battery < 20:
    print("Low battery")
    battery = 100
print("Battery:", battery)

options.rationale: `35 < 20` is false, so the whole block is skipped, including the assignment.
The block only runs when the condition is true, and `35 < 20` is false.
Both indented lines belong to the block, so neither the message nor the reset runs.
`battery = 100` is indented, so it is part of the skipped block and never runs.

explanation: `35 < 20` is `False`, so Python jumps over both indented lines. `battery` keeps its old value, and only the unindented last line runs: `Battery: 35`.

stem: What is the output of the following code?

options.rationale: A list counts as true only when it has items; `[]` is falsy.
With `if-else`, exactly one of the two blocks always runs, so something is printed before `Items: 0`.

options.text:
Ready to pay
Your basket is empty
Items: 0
options.rationale: `if` and `else` never both run; exactly one branch is chosen.
An empty list is falsy, so the `else` block runs, and the last line always runs.

explanation: The condition is the list itself. An empty list `[]` counts as false (truthiness), so the `if` block is skipped and the `else` block prints `Your basket is empty`. The last line is not indented, so it runs either way and prints `Items: 0`.

stem: What happens when you run this code?
code:
pages = 120
if pages == 120
    print("A short book")

options.rationale: The condition is true, but Python cannot run the code at all because the `if` line has no colon.

options.text: Nothing is printed, and the program ends without an error
options.rationale: Python does report a problem: it checks the syntax before running anything, finds the missing colon and stops with an error.

options.text: Nothing is printed: Python reports a `SyntaxError`
options.rationale: Every `if` line must end with a colon. Python checks this before running any line, so not even `pages = 120` runs.
The indentation is fine; the problem is the missing `:` at the end of the `if` line, which is `SyntaxError: expected ':'`.

explanation: An `if` statement is the keyword `if`, a condition and a colon. Without the colon, Python stops with `SyntaxError: expected ':'` before any line runs.

stem: What is the output of the following code?

options.rationale: `"1234"` is a string and `1234` is an int; `==` compares type as well as digits, so they are not equal.
A string is never equal to an int, so the condition is false and the `else` block runs.
With `if-else`, only one of the two blocks runs.
The condition is worked out to choose a branch; its value is not printed.

explanation: `code` holds the string `"1234"`. Comparing it with the int `1234` gives `False`, because values of different types like these are never equal. The `if` block is skipped and the `else` block prints `Wrong code`.

stem: Which statement about an `if-else` statement is true?

options.text: Both blocks run when the condition is true.
options.rationale: The `else` block only runs when the condition is false.

options.text: The `else` line needs its own condition, such as `else x < 5:`.
options.rationale: `else` never takes a condition; it catches every case the `if` did not.

options.text: If the condition is false, neither block runs.
options.rationale: That is true for an `if` without `else`. With `else`, the `else` block runs when the condition is false.

options.text: Exactly one of its two blocks runs each time it is reached.
options.rationale: If the condition is true the `if` block runs, otherwise the `else` block runs: never both, never neither.

explanation: `if-else` chooses between two paths. The condition is checked once: when it is `True` the `if` block runs, and when it is `False` the `else` block runs. `else` is written as `else:` with no condition.

stem: Complete the code so that a 15-year-old is told to wait, and the program prints `Wait until you are 16`.
code:
age = 15
if age __BLANK1__ 16:
    print("You may get a learner's permit")
__BLANK2__:
    print("Wait until you are 16")

blanks.rationale: Only people aged 16 or more may get the permit, so the test is `age >= 16`, which is false for 15.
The second path has no condition of its own, so it starts with `else:`.

explanation: `15 >= 16` is `False`, so the `if` block is skipped and the `else` block runs. With `<`, `<=` or `!=`, the condition would be true for 15 and the permit message would print instead.

stem: Which line, inserted at the marked spot, makes the program print `Sold out`?
code:
stock = 0
# >>> INSERT <<<
    print("Sold out")
else:
    print("In stock:", stock)

options.rationale: `0 == 0` is `True`, so the `if` block prints `Sold out`.
`0` is falsy, so this sends the program to the `else` block.
`0 > 0` is `False`, so the `else` block runs and prints `In stock: 0`.
`0 != 0` is `False`, which picks the `else` block.

explanation: The `if` block must run when there is no stock. `stock == 0` is `True` for 0. The other conditions are all false for 0, so they would choose the `else` block.
